newsitem.title: USA: Icahn sells RJR Nabisco stake.
newsitem.headline: Icahn sells RJR Nabisco stake.

text.p: Carl Icahn said Thursday that he sold his stock in RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. and has abandoned, at least for now, a more than year-long effort to break up the giant food and tobacco company.

Icahn sold his 19.9 million shares at $36.75 apiece in an off-market deal handled by Goldman Sachs, a trade that reaped him more than $130 million in profit and in effect nullified his proxy fight to replace the RJR board at the annual meeting in April, according to analysts.
The buyer or buyers were not identified but were thought to be a group of institutions and investment funds.
The stake equalled about 7.3 percent of New York-based RJR, which makes Winston and Salem brand cigarettes, Oreo cookies, Ritz crackers, Lifesavers candy and other products.

In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Icahn said it would be "exceedingly difficult" to win a fight for control of RJR now but that he may relaunch a proxy fight if the price of its stock falls.
But industry analysts said Icahn was unlikely to spar with RJR management again.

"He isn't coming back. He is a smart guy who had the guts to buy the stock," said Gary Black, tobacco analyst at Sanford C. Bernstein. "It's another chapter in his book on how to make money on undervalued companies."
Icahn also said in the statement that he does not see the current tobacco litigation climate improving, meaning the current RJR board may not spin off the company's Nabisco Holdings Corp. subsidiary.
RJR, which owns 80.5 percent of Nabisco Holdings, has repeatedly said it would spin off the food company at what it deemed the appropriate time.

Icahn started his campaign to force a spin-off in 1995 when he teamed up with investor Bennett LeBow, whose Brooke Group Ltd. last year became the first cigarette maker to settle lawsuits against the tobacco industry.
Icahn and LeBow's bid to force an immediate spin-off failed last year and the investors split after the defeat.
They said a spin-off would unlock value in the food company, which under the current ownership structure has been hurt by concerns about the tobacco business.
Icahn resumed his effort to force a breakup last November when he nominated a slate of directors to replace existing board members at RJR Nabisco Holdings.

"He is no longer a shareholder, so now he can't even get into the annual meeting. He is all done. He accomplished his objective, which was to make a living, to have a good year," said Emanuel Goldman, tobacco analyst at PainWebber.
Some analysts said Icahn's departure could hasten a settlement of huge liability claims against cigarette makers.
They noted that RJR Chairman Steven Goldstone is involved in negotiations with anti-smoking groups to settle the lawsuits.
"These are very delicate talks and if Icahn was successful in taking over the RJR board, he could have toppled the applecart," said Martin Feldman at Smith Barney.

Analysts also said LeBow's position has been weakened without Icahn also pushing for a spin-off, though he is less likely to sell his roughly 1 percent of RJR now because he bought at a higher price than Icahn's average $30 a share.
Calls to LeBow and Icahn were not returned. Goldman Sachs declined to provide addtional details on the huge trade.
RJR Nabisco's stock fell $1.125 to $36.625 and Nabisco Holdings lost $1.375 to $42 on the NYSE.
Among other tobacco stocks, Philip Morris rose $2 to $135.50, UST added 50 cents to $30.25 and Brooke ended unchanged at $5, all in consolidated NYSE trading.
B.A.T Industries Plc's U.S.-traded shares fell 44 cents to $17.75 on the American Stock Exchange.
